vignette:
Sione, a 51-year-old married man of Oceanian descent, presented to the clinic describing a persistent struggle since a severe motor vehicle collision three years prior. A welder by trade, Sione had always prided himself on his steady hands and calm demeanor, qualities that now felt distant, replaced by an unsettling vigilance that permeated every aspect of his life.

The accident itself had been a horrific blur. He remembered driving home late one evening when a drunk driver, speeding and swerving erratically, veered directly into his lane. The sickening crunch of metal, the screech of tires, the shattering glass – it all happened in an instant. Sione’s vehicle was T-boned, his body violently thrown against the interior, leaving him with multiple fractures and internal injuries. The overwhelming smell of alcohol from the other driver's wrecked car lingered in the air as he lay trapped, convinced he was bleeding to death. It was a life-threatening ordeal from which he was lucky to escape alive, though the physical and emotional scars remained.

Now, three years on, the event was far from a distant memory. When the memories of what happened came to mind, Sione found himself completely reliving the moment. It wasn't just a mental image; it was a full sensory reliving, where he could smell the gasoline and alcohol, hear the screeching metal, and feel the impact again as if it were happening in real time. These intrusions were particularly distressing because when the memory returned, he felt physical pain in the same parts of his body as during the event, a phantom agony in his ribs and leg that mimicked his injuries. More disturbingly, he often felt his body was in the same position as when the frightening event occurred, contorted and trapped, even when he was safe in his own home. This constant, vivid replay of the event meant that any sensory input even remotely resembling aspects of the accident became an immediate and overwhelming trigger for his distress.

It was this intensely real, bodily reenactment of his trauma that made his daily life so fraught. The vividness and physical immediacy of his memories meant that even the slightest external cue could plunge him back into the collision. For instance, the sound of car sounds, particularly sudden braking or the rumble of heavy vehicles passing his workshop, could instantly trigger a wave of dread and the sensation of impact. Similarly, seeing crash imagery, even just a crumpled fender on a television show or a damaged car on the road, would flood his mind with the horrific scene of his own accident. And the olfactory trigger of alcohol smell, whether from a spilled drink at a family gathering or a passing stranger, was enough to bring back the metallic taste of fear and the sensation of choking on fumes.

Sione’s work as a welder, once a source of pride, had become a minefield. The constant hum of machinery, the clanking of metal, and the proximity to vehicles and their parts at the fabrication shop made him perpetually on edge. He found himself meticulously inspecting every vehicle that entered the shop, a ritual born from the fear that another crash was imminent. He started taking longer routes home, avoiding busy intersections and highways, even if it meant adding an hour to his commute. His wife, perplexed by his increasing withdrawal and irritability, had tried to understand, but Sione struggled to articulate the terror that gripped him. He knew he was isolating himself, cancelling social engagements and retreating into himself, convinced that by staying home, he was protecting himself from unseen dangers. He even stopped his weekly visits to his brother, which used to be a highlight, because the drive was too overwhelming.

He finally sought help because the exhaustion of constant vigilance was overwhelming him, and he could no longer bear the thought of his children seeing him so diminished. He feared he was losing himself completely, trapped in a cycle where the past was relentlessly invading the present, and he desperately wanted to find a way back to the man he once was.
